analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies at Canadian prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 25 Senate supporters, all Democrats and one Independent, it was sent to the Senate health committee in January 2019 and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the FDA to write rules within 180 days allowing wholesalers, pharmacies, and individual patients to import prescription drugs from Canada. The same drug, made in the same FDA-approved factories, often sells for far less in Canada because the Canadian government negotiates prices. The bill set up a certification system for foreign pharmacies, required testing and safety checks, banned manufacturers from retaliating against Canadian sellers who export to Americans, and after two years could have expanded importation to other developed countries. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high prices for prescription drugs, especially people on fixed incomes taking long-term medications like insulin, which the bill explicitly covered. Wholesalers and pharmacies that could import and sell the same drugs at lower cost would also have gained.

how_it_helps.text: Required the FDA to allow wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals to import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada within 180 days of enactment.
Let individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply from certified foreign pharmacies with a valid US prescription, and specifically included insulin and dialysis solution for individual importers.
After two years, if importation from Canada showed real savings and safety, the Secretary could extend importation to any OECD country with comparable drug-approval standards.

Made it unlawful for manufacturers to charge Canadian exporters more than Canadian customers, to cut off supply to certified sellers, or to alter products to dodge importation — closing the main ways drug companies could block the program.

Built in safety protections: only licensed, long-established foreign pharmacies could participate, labs would randomly test imports for chemical authenticity, and the FDA could immediately suspend importation of any drug, seller, or importer showing a pattern of counterfeit or recalled products.
Added criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine for websites selling adulterated or counterfeit drugs to Americans.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the price difference between the US market and Canada on drugs sold to Americans through importers. The certification program would be paid for by fees on foreign sellers.

drawbacks.text: The core good-faith objection: critics argue that opening imports raises the risk of counterfeit or substandard drugs reaching patients, even with testing and certification, since enforcement against foreign sellers is harder than against domestic ones. The bill's heavy safety architecture — certification, testing labs, suspension powers, criminal penalties — shows its own sponsors took this risk seriously.

Canada's drug market is far smaller than the US market, so large-scale importation could strain the Canadian supply and pull medication away from Canadian patients. The bill tried to manage this by banning manufacturers from restricting supply to exporters, but relied on untested enforcement mechanisms.

The bill depended on the Secretary of Health and Human Services writing regulations and on manufacturers not finding workarounds (such as reformulating drugs for different markets), so its real-world savings were not guaranteed by the text alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for patients is large: the same FDA-manufactured pills routinely cost a fraction of US prices in Canada, and the bill covered exactly the drugs people struggle to afford, including insulin. The safety risks are real but were directly addressed with certification, testing, recall rules, and criminal penalties, so the main uncertainty is enforcement and supply, not the concept. A reasonable person could still prefer tighter pilot programs, but the bill's death was driven by the industries that would pay for lower prices, not by an inability to answer the safety objections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on January 10, 2019 with 24 cosponsors — 23 Democrats and one Independent — and no Republicans.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken; the bill sat in committee for the entire two-year Congress and expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept charging Americans US prices while charging Canadians far less for the identical products, and patients kept paying the difference.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 23 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Booker, Brown, Klobuchar, Manchin, Warren, and Whitehouse.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed in committee for the full Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill or similar drug importation measures to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA and brand-name drug makers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed prescription drug importation legislation, arguing it endangered safety and undermined drug pricing.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; not one of the Senate's Republicans signed on, and the Republican chair and majority never moved the bill.

industries.note: Importation would let Americans buy the same FDA-manufactured drugs at Canadian prices, erasing the gap between the two markets, and the bill made it illegal to charge exporters more or cut off supply to block the program. Their gain under the status quo is the higher price US patients pay.
Importers could buy qualifying drugs abroad and dispense them at lower prices, attracting patients priced out of domestic supplies. Their interest runs with patients' interest in cheaper drugs.
Certified foreign sellers would gain a large new customer base in American patients, paying a user fee to fund the certification and enforcement program.
